planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade to partial shade; this German selection was bred specifically for heavier flower production than typical Vinca minor.

directions: Marie is a German-raised periwinkle selection bred for a notably heavier flush of bright violet-blue, windmill-shaped flowers than the species typically produces, opening over small glossy dark-green leaves in mid-spring with a lighter repeat often appearing in fall. Plant it in evenly moist, humus-rich soil under shade to light shade, where its trailing stems root as they spread to knit into a dense evergreen mat. Established plantings need only occasional watering during dry stretches and benefit from an early-spring shearing every few years to keep flowering stems vigorous. It is a reliable choice for underplanting shrubs or edging shaded paths where bloom display matters more than foliage variegation.

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring or early fall into average, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this vigorous clone forms a tight weed-suppressing carpet under trees and along shaded slopes.

directions: Kronstadt is a long-cultivated European strain of barren strawberry selected for flowers distinctly larger than the species, opening bright yellow above glossy, strawberry-like evergreen trifoliate leaves in mid-spring. It spreads steadily by rhizomes to form a dense, low mat well suited to covering the base of trees, shaded slopes, or neglected corners where little else thrives. Give it ordinary garden soil with reasonable drainage in partial to full shade; established plantings tolerate short dry spells but perform best with occasional watering through summer. Unlike more aggressive spreaders it stays well-behaved near choicer woodland companions, needing only an occasional trim to keep edges tidy.

common_name: Minor Dwarf Mondo Grass (Tiniest of the Dwarf Lilyturfs)

planting.note: Plant small divisions in spring into well-drained soil in partial shade; this is the smallest and slowest of the dwarf mondo selections, so give extra time to fill in compared with 'Nana'.

directions: This is the smallest dwarf mondo grass in general cultivation, forming tufts of dark green, grass-like evergreen foliage barely an inch or two tall and creeping outward at roughly an inch per year, far slower than the already-dwarf 'Nana'. Small white flowers hide among the leaves in summer, followed by sky-blue berries. Its extreme slowness and tiny scale make it best suited to miniature landscapes: tucking between flagstones, lining a narrow path edge, or filling the rim of a container rather than covering open ground. Grow it in well-drained soil with regular water through the growing season in dappled sun to partial shade, and expect it to need years rather than seasons to knit together.

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring into well-drained soil in partial shade to sun; this Australian-bred selection is marketed as a low-growing lawn alternative, cut back once a year rather than regularly mowed.

directions: Silverlawn is an Australian breeding-program selection of lily turf, discovered in Oakville, New South Wales, and notable for leaf striping distinctly wider and whiter than typical variegated liriope, giving the clump an overall silvery cast when viewed from a distance rather than the more common thin-edged variegation. Compact spikes of lilac flowers rise above the foliage in summer. It is marketed as a low-growing lawn alternative for foot-traffic areas, needing only an annual winter cutback rather than regular mowing to stay dense and tidy. Plant it in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, watering regularly through its first season and tapering off once the clump is established.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist, humus-rich woodland soil in shade; this Don Jacobs/Eco Gardens selection carpets more densely and rapidly than typical wild Asarum canadense.

directions: Eco Choice is a selection made by the late plantsman Don Jacobs of Eco Gardens, chosen for noticeably faster, denser carpeting growth than wild-collected Asarum canadense. Rounded to heart-shaped, softly fuzzy deciduous leaves two to four inches across form a tight colony, hiding the odd, starfish-shaped brownish flowers that nestle at ground level beneath the foliage in spring. It spreads readily by shallow rhizomes in consistently moist, rich woodland soil, making it a quicker-filling option than the species for carpeting beneath shade trees. Keep soil evenly moist through the growing season; the deciduous foliage dies back cleanly with fall frost and re-emerges reliably each spring.

common_name: Crug's Cover Chinese Spurge (Crûg Farm Collection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in shade; raised from a Crûg Farm Plants seed collection made in Sichuan, China in 2000, this selection tolerates both heavy shade and drier soil than most pachysandra.

directions: Crug's Cover grew from a seed collection Crûg Farm Plants made in Sichuan, China in 2000 and was named for its mat-forming spread on short, flexible suckering stems carrying polished, undulate, leathery evergreen leaves. In late winter it produces short dense spikes of heavily fragrant creamy-white flowers tucked beneath the foliage, with a scent recalling Sarcococca, later followed by pink berries tipped with odd horn-like styles. It is notably tolerant of both deep shade and drier soil than typical pachysandra, making it useful under mature trees where irrigation is inconsistent. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil and expect a slow but steady spread into a low, dense evergreen cover over several seasons.

common_name: Texas Too Tall Sensitive Fern (Giant Wetland Selection)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring into moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial sun to light shade; collected from a boggy Texas site, it grows notably taller than typical sensitive fern and spreads by rhizome in damp ground.

directions: Collected in 2004 from a boggy site in Cass County, Texas, and introduced by Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden in 2009, this sensitive fern selection grows noticeably larger than the typical species, reaching up to roughly three and a half feet tall in half-day sun versus the usual two-foot height. Broad, deeply cut deciduous fronds emerge on red-tinged stipes each spring and spread steadily by creeping rhizome through consistently wet ground, making it well suited to rain gardens, pond margins, or other low spots that stay damp through the season. Give it rich, evenly moist to wet soil in partial sun to light shade for the largest fronds. Like the species, foliage collapses completely at the first hard frost and the clump re-emerges reliably the following spring.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden
